newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan president tries to calm angry voters.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan president tries to calm angry voters.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Violeta Chamorro on Tuesday urged "hot heads" angry over election results not to resort to violence as delays in announcing the official winners threatened to spark unrest.
Nine days after Nicaraguans went to the polls, the Supreme Election Council has still not announced the official outcome of the presidential, legislative and mayoral elections.
The left-wing Sandinistas have questioned preliminary results that show the right-wing Liberal Alliance led by Arnoldo Aleman won the presidential race by a wide margin.
"We had a civic festival with a marvellous election. It was something beautiful. How can we lose it now?" Chamorro, a centrist, told reporters.
Her comments came as police banned public demonstrations for fear of bloodshed after two mayoral candidates in the capital each claimed victory.

Surrounded by hundreds of his left-wing supporters, Carlos Guadamuz, the maverick director of Sandinista-owned Radio Ya, announced on Monday that he had won the vote for Managua mayor based on a recount of the votes by his party.
The Sandinista Front has complained the original count, which put Guadamuz behind Liberal Roberto Cedeno, had "serious irregularities" and hinted at fraud by their rivals.

President Chamorro and the Catholic Church have urged the CSE to hurry up and announce the winners as simmering tempers threaten to boil over, fed by rumours of fraud and premature victory celebrations.

"Why don't they ease the tension as quickly as possible so that all Nicaraguans can know who their next president is going to be," she said, adding that the official results of the vote would likely not be known till mid-November.
In the presidential race, preliminary results put Aleman, a fiercely anti-Sandinista former mayor of Managua, ahead of former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega by 49 to 38 percent.
But Ortega, who led the 1979-1990 Sandinista government, has refused to concede defeat, saying the count is invalid and he will wait for the result of the CSE's review of the voting.
Tensions rose on Monday when Guadamuz, in an address on his radio station, called on his Sandinista supporters to defend his self-proclaimed victory to the "last consequences."
Angry callers to Radio Ya said they would not stand idly by and let Aleman's Liberal Alliance rob them of victory through election fraud, threatening popular insurrection.
"The Liberal Somocistas (supporters of the former dictator Somoza) are trying to rob us again, but we will defend our victory with arms if we have to," said caller Andrea Romero.
As hundreds of Guadamuz supporters gathered around Radio Ya headquarters to celebrate his victory, National Police called for calm and banned demonstrations.

"We are worried by the intense climate of instability being created by the announcers of Radio Ya, who are practically calling for subversion against the authorities," said Cedeno, who continued to affirm his lead in vote.
Right-wing Radio Corporacion answered Radio Ya's diatribes by fiercely defending Cedeno's victory and warning of conflict if the Sandinista demands continued.

The rapidly escalating tensions underscored the lingering polarisation that haunts Nicaragua nearly seven years after its civil war between right-wing Contra rebels and the Marxist Sandinista government ended.
